The Cuban grassquit (Phonipara canora) begins life as a yolk-dependent embryo encased in a calcareous egg, with incubation proceeding at a temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, which are typical of shaded nest sites in the species' Caribbean habitat, the embryo completes organogenesis and hatches after roughly 12 days [ab = roughly 12 days] at a temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C]. This relatively brief incubation period is consistent with the rapid developmental schedules observed in other small-bodied Neotropical finches. Upon hatching, the altricial nestling emerges at a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.96 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.96 grams], a modest initial mass that reflects the limited yolk reserves available to a passerine embryo of this size. This neonatal mass is notably smaller than that reported for the larger congeneric Geospiza fortis, scaled in proportion to the substantial difference in adult body size between the two species. The hatchling, dependent entirely on parental provisioning, begins the exotrophic transition as the parents deliver insect prey and seeds to the nest.

As the nestling chick develops within the brooded environment of the nest, it undergoes a rapid phase of mass gain, ultimately reaching a maximum adult body mass in females of about 8.1 grams [Wwi = about 8.1 grams]. This ultimate wet weight for females is typical for a bird of this lineage and represents the asymptotic mass attained after the completion of somatic growth. The growing juvenile progresses through the pin-feathered stage to full plumage, and the achievement of flight feather maturation marks a critical developmental milestone. Under the active metabolic conditions characteristic of the species, typically recorded at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the nestling departs the nest at a fledging age of approximately 13 days after hatching [tx = approximately 13 days after hatching]. This timing of first flight achievement is derived from comparative data on Geospiza fortis and reflects the altricial strategy of the Cuban grassquit, wherein the fledgling is capable of short flights before it attains full independence from its parents.

The post-fledging period involves a gradual transition as the young individual shifts from parental provisioning to nutritional independence. The juvenile bird continues to refine its foraging skills, and the onset of gonadal activity signals the approach of reproductive maturity. Under the sustained thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] that typifies the active metabolic state of this passerine, puberty is reached at approximately 39 days after hatching [tp = approximately 39 days after hatching]. This relatively early attainment of sexual maturation is consistent with the fast life-history strategy of many small tropical finches, which begin breeding shortly after completing their own growth. The pre-reproductive period is therefore brief, allowing the species to capitalize on favorable seasonal conditions for the production of offspring. Field data suggest that a combination of high metabolic demand and abundant food resources drives this accelerated developmental schedule.

The onset of breeding activity in the Cuban grassquit reflects the species' capacity for multiple nesting attempts within a single season. First breeding typically occurs at about 343 days after hatching [tR = about 343 days after hatching], a timing that corresponds to the first reproductive event observed in wild populations maintained at an ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This age at first reproduction allows the bird to time its initial clutch with the peak availability of insect prey and grass seeds. The maximum reproductive output of the species is characterized by a combination of moderate clutch sizes and repeated nesting efforts. Females produce a clutch of 2 to 3 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = 2 to 3 eggs per nesting attempt] and can complete as many as three clutches in a single year [F_R_i = three clutches in a single year] under the warm thermal conditions typical of this species.

The maximum longevity of the Cuban grassquit in the wild, estimated from field records of banded individuals, reaches approximately 8.4 years [am = approximately 8.4 years] when the birds are active at the characteristic body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This lifespan is comparable to that of other small granivorous finches in the Caribbean region and reflects the trade-off between high annual reproductive effort and survival. The resting metabolic rate, measured in respirometry trials, averages about 28 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = about 28 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at the same temperature, a value that is typical for a bird of 8.1 grams bod at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]y mass. This relatively elevated metabolic rate supports the high activity levels and rapid development observed throughout the life cycle of Phonipara canora, from the brief incubation period through the accelerated attainment of sexual maturation and the repeated nesting efforts that define its reproductive life history.
